articles.title: Global Bond Selloff Sends 10-Year Treasury Yields to Cusp of 5%
articles.summary: Bond bears are pushing benchmark Treasury yields toward the closely-watched 5% level ahead of US inflation data that stands to determine expectations for a F...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Bond bears are pushing benchmark Treasury yields toward the closely-watched 5% level ahead of US inflation data that stands to determine expectations for a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike next week.

The yield on 10-year notes climbed 18 basis points this week to trade just below the psychologically-important level, which may attract dip buyers but also risks triggering further selling that could spill over into global markets. At 4.96% on Friday, the yield has reached the most-elevated level since 2023 — and is approaching its highest since 2007.

The surge in yields comes as traders wrestle with rising oil prices and inflation that's run above the Federal Reserve's target for half a decade. A reading of the US consumer price index Friday stands to be one of the most pivotal in years as traders price in a roughly 70% chance of a rate increase at the Sept. 16 Fed meeting.

"Hitting 5% on the 10-year Treasury yield looks more like an inevitability here than a forecast," said Padhraic Garvey, head of research for the Americas at ING Groep NV. "These are worrying times for bond markets."

Yields on the two-year, which are more sensitive to Fed rate moves, rose to as high as 4.59% this week. Thirty-year yields hit their highest since 2007, luring standout demand at an auction of the securities.

The moves have spilled over into bond markets worldwide, with Australian benchmark yields hitting their highest since 2011 on Friday and Japanese equivalents trading close to the key psychological level of 3%. A gauge of global yields is at its highest since 2007.

"A lower US CPI and a Fed hike are really the only circuit breakers I see at this point, otherwise I don't think anyone is comfortable being long rates," said Michael Tang, a rates strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia in Sydney. "It's just massive hawkish sentiment taking over."

That leaves traders on edge going into Friday's main economic event — especially as Fed officials have underscored their focus on inflation in recent weeks. To Molly Brooks, a US rates strategist at TD Securities, a hotter-than-expected print stands to boost market expectations for a hike in September and additional tightening.

articles.title: Even a cooler inflation report may not be enough to keep the Fed from raising rates next week
articles.summary: Americans have already been feeling the pain at the gas pump as the war with Iran has pushed up prices to record highs for this time of year. But the bigger...
articles.body:
Americans have already been feeling the pain at the gas pump as the war with Iran has pushed up prices to record highs for this time of year. But the bigger concern is what happens next.

Persistently higher energy prices – especially for diesel – could continue to push up the cost of freight and become inescapable for businesses, making groceries and other consumer goods more expensive.

That's why the Federal Reserve is watching Friday's August Consumer Price Index report even more closely than usual. The latest report is expected to show that inflation cooled slightly on an annual basis — but economists also expect prices to have picked up on a monthly basis. Any hint that price pressures remain stubborn or have broadened across the economy could be enough to convince Fed officials to hike interest rates at next week's monetary policy meeting.

Economists polled by FactSet expect inflation for the 12 months ended in August to come in at 3.3%, a slight deceleration from July's 3.4% rate. On a monthly basis, though, price increases are expected to accelerate to 0.4%, compared to July's 0.1% pace.

When stripping out food and energy prices, a measure of underlying inflation known as "core" inflation is expected to remain relatively tame. Economists expect core prices to rise by 0.2% in August, unchanged from July, bringing the annual rate down to 2.4% from the prior month.

But the headline and core numbers may not tell the full story.

Wholesale inflation as measured by the Producer Price Index accelerated sharply in August, according to the latest report, released Thursday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Prices for goods alone rose 1.1% last month, a significant shift from July's 0.4% decline. More than three-quarters of that increase was driven by a 4.2% monthly rise in energy prices, the BLS said.

PPI is seen as an important indicator for how consumer prices could move in coming months, since businesses are typically the first to see price increases. But higher costs aren't necessarily passed along to shoppers, since many businesses absorb some of the increase themselves.

That could become harder to do if businesses are squeezed by higher tariffs at the same time that elevated energy costs are pushing up the cost of transportation.

Corporate America is 'covered' — for now

If you ship a package right now with a carrier like UPS, you'll pay a fuel surcharge that's adjusted weekly, based on average fuel prices tracked by the government.

Big corporations, however, often negotiate longer-term contracts with carriers that lock in their transportation rates, shielding them from some of the immediate impact when fuel and other transportation costs rise.

articles.title: America can’t grow its way out of its debt problem
articles.summary: The US economy is staring down the barrel of $40 trillion in debt, bond yields on the cusp of a 19-year high and a costly war driving inflation higher. The T...
articles.body:
The US economy is staring down the barrel of $40 trillion in debt, bond yields on the cusp of a 19-year high and a costly war driving inflation higher. The Trump administration has a novel solution: We'll just grow our way out of the problem.

It's a refrain President Donald Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have used frequently in recent weeks. It's an effort to calm a market that has grown increasingly nervous about the war in Iran and Washington's lack of a coherent plan to get its fiscal house in order.

The administration's theory is grounded in a degree of real economic theory : If the US economy grows at a significantly faster rate, its debt would eventually become relatively sustainable.

But to accomplish that, America's economy would need to grow at a faster rate for many years. That's not something any administration can control. And the idea assumes we won't keep adding massively to our debt, a theory belied by populist economic policies supported by politicians on both sides of the aisle.

That's why the market isn't buying it. The math just doesn't math. Inflation is making a comeback , spending is out of control, and Washington has no political will to fix either problem.

America's debt crossing the $40 trillion mark last month sounded a number of alarm bells. But the most pressing question is whether – and how long – we can keep running massive deficits.

When economists try to determine whether the government's debt is sustainable, a common metric they look to is the difference between "g" (the economy's growth rate, or GDP) and "r" (the rate of interest on the debt, or 10-year Treasury yields).

When g is bigger than r , the debt becomes relatively insignificant compared to economic growth. When r is bigger than g , the debt can grow at an unsustainable pace.

That seems self-evident: If you keep getting a raise year after year and you're able to pay the interest on your debt today, you'll be able to pay it in the future, too – and it'll become easier to pay it down as your paycheck grows.

Economies don't function quite like consumers or businesses, and economists debate what "sustainable" debt looks like. But right now, r is around 5%, and g is around 2%. That, at the very least, raises the risk that America's debt is on an unsustainable path.

But that's not the only metric flashing a warning about America's debt burden. The primary deficit – the difference between an economy's spending and tax revenue, minus interest payments – is also a concern.

articles.title: 25 years after 9/11, airport security gets second look from Trump
articles.summary: The 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks falls as the Trump administration has scaled back expanded security measures put in place at airports across the nation to prevent terrorists from using planes against the U.S. ever again. The hijacking of planes ushered in a new era of screenings, while even more restrictive measures…
articles.body:
The 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks falls as the Trump administration has scaled back expanded security measures put in place at airports across the nation to prevent terrorists from using planes against the U.S. ever again.

The hijacking of planes ushered in a new era of screenings, while even more restrictive measures were enacted on shoes and liquids that could be brought onto a plane in the wake of later foiled plots.

While those measures may have helped prevent another 9/11-like attack, the security constraints were also subjects of irritation for millions of travelers.

Under President Trump, the administration has reduced some of the restrictions, eliminating the requirement to remove shoes for screening and launching a pilot program to allow non-ticketed passengers to pass through security in some airports. They are also weighing whether to remove restrictions on liquid volumes for those with TSA PreCheck.

Jamil Jaffer, founder of the National Security Institute at George Mason University’s Antonin Scalia Law School, said advancements in screening technology have allowed agents at the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to more deeply examine what’s in bags or could potentially be concealed on the body.

“There’s some things you can do that you couldn’t do in the past that technology allows you to get to. So that’s one reason you might be able to change the rules,” said Jaffer, who cited an “evolution in technology.”

“While one of those things may not be the straw that breaks the proverbial camel’s back, it could be that if we do all these things simultaneously and we take our eye off the ball, it could be that a terrorist attack is successful.”

The anniversary comes as the threat picture facing the U.S. has shifted in some areas.

While the U.S. has concluded wars in Iraq and Afghanistan launched in the aftermath of 9/11, Trump has reinserted the U.S. into the Middle East, launching attacks in Iran.

At the same time, national security experts in recent years have repeatedly warned of the risk from lone wolf attacks, including those that may be inspired by foreign terrorist groups. Recent attacks have focused on facilities that do not have as much security as an airport.

Former Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem was the first to dismantle a post-9/11 security screening, giving the order to end the requirement that passengers remove their shoes.

Though popular, the move set off alarm bells with DHS’s Office of Inspector General, which in a letter obtained by The Wall Street Journal found that the full body scanners used across the country were not always able to see through shoes.

Noem faced backlash from Democrats in Congress who said she rushed the decision and failed to fully consult with TSA, but the move raised questions over whether she would lift other policies — like limitations on liquids.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.), ranking member of the House Homeland Security Committee, said the administration has rebuffed their efforts to conduct oversight over the change in the shoe policy, leaving uncertainty about the safety of that move and whether future policy changes will be rigorously evaluated.

“Reports indicate the Trump administration changed TSA’s shoe policy for political reasons, creating a completely unnecessary security gap, which is compounded by the increased threats from Trump’s unnecessary War in Iran,” Thompson said in a statement.

“The Trump administration continues to block congressional oversight of TSA’s shoe policy change and refuses to adjust it in light of reported vulnerabilities.”

Still, DHS is looking at other changes, albeit with the smaller population of passengers who use TSA PreCheck and therefore have already been vetted.

That includes the launch at just 13 airports of a program to allow those without tickets or travel plans to pass through security to accompany travelers.

Reports this week also indicated TSA might similarly allow PreCheck passengers to enter the airport with water, citing new technology that can distinguish water from other liquids.

Stewart Verdery, a former DHS official during the George W. Bush administration, said after 9/11 “we had to build basically a whole new security apparatus from scratch.”

“It was this one-size-fits-all set of rules for everybody … there was no differentiation of travelers at all; there was basically just everyone was treated as the same type of threat,” he said.

But that’s evolved with programs like Clear and PreCheck, which he called the system’s first effort at “risk differentiation.”

“It takes some political courage to turn off something that’s uniform and make it more risk-based, and that’s hard to get people — if they’re thinking of a zero-tolerance type of system — to do,” he said.

Americans’ tolerance for airport screenings has also been complex. On one hand, the public expects rigorous security, but they have also grumbled about having to remove their shoes or not being able to travel with preferred toiletries.

Verdery noted that TSA is expected to screen every passenger and find any potential threat — a standard of perfection not expected of any other DHS agency.

“Think of the Coast Guard. I mean, they’re not expected to find every drug boat, right? Or the border patrol is not expected to arrest every migrant. So, the zero tolerance is really only for TSA, which is an interesting conundrum for them to try to live under,” he said.

Verdery applauded making changes for the population that already has TSA PreCheck, noting that they have been vetted through government databases.

“The more risk differentiation we can build the system, the better. So the people that are going through PreCheck or going through Global Entry, those types of things — they ought to be treated differently. They’ve volunteered to be vetted every single day,” he said.

Jaffer said as the U.S. weighs its security risks, it cannot forget the broader terrorist network

“The most effective thing that we can do against terrorism, it’s probably not necessarily the passenger screening. It’s probably remaining on offense against terrorists overseas and hitting them where they build up their camps, where they’ve got training facilities, where they’re recruiting folks,” he said.

He noted that Iran remains a top sponsor of terrorist groups and that the adversary could weigh terrorist attacks as part of their strategy in the ongoing war.

“Terrorists still very much want to attack the United States. They still want to kill Americans. They still want to kill Western allies. They have not stopped. They’ve not stopped trying. They’ve not stopped planning,” he said.

“You have to realize that there is very much a desire on the part of the adversary to continue to come after us.”

articles.title: France lowers growth forecast, will miss deficit target
articles.summary: By Leigh Thomas PARIS, Sept 11 (Reuters) - France's economy will grow less than expected this year and the government will miss its budget deficit target, Fi...
articles.body:
PARIS, Sept 11 (Reuters) - France's economy will grow less than expected this year and the government will miss its budget deficit target, Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Friday.

The downgraded outlook complicates the government's ‌task of getting its 2027 budget passed in the coming months in a deeply divided parliament, where parties have ‌hardened their positions before an April-May two-round presidential election.

Lescure told journalists he was lowering the government's 2026 economic growth forecast to 0.5% from 0.7% previously, but stuck ​with a projection of 1.0% for next year.

"This year has been marked by extreme crises involving four different types of shocks," Lescure told reporters, citing domestic political uncertainty, surging energy prices, extreme summer weather and a jump in borrowing costs on bond markets.

Slower growth will make it more difficult for the government to trim its fiscal budget deficit as planned to 5.0% of economic output ‌this year.

"The reality is that the budget ⁠was built on a 5% assumption. And the reality is that, today, 5% is no longer an option," Lescure said.

The minister did not give a new deficit target, adding that the government was still ⁠making final tweaks to its budget bill, which it is due to present to parliament at the end of the month.

As the government's deficit target has slipped out of reach, France has seen the risk premium it must pay to borrow for 10 years versus the German government ​widen ​to the most since 2012.

With polls suggesting next year's presidential election could ​see a run-off between far-right candidate Marine Le ‌Pen and the hard left's Jean-Luc Melenchon, investors say there is still scope for more intense bond market tensions.

"I think we are at the foothills of something more concerning for France," James Athey, fixed income manager at Marlborough in London, told Reuters. "The spread at the moment is not pricing all the risks. It is not pricing a Le Pen or Melenchon presidency."

The economic fallout from the war in the Middle East and summer heatwaves and drought that hit agriculture output have dragged down growth and ‌put the government's fiscal targets out of reach.

"I think it is reasonable ​to say that economic uncertainty has never been greater than it is today," ​Lescure said. "We are operating under tight budgetary constraints; there is ​no more fat to trim."

Further complicating the picture, French borrowing rates have surged in recent weeks as ‌investors have identified France as one of the weaker ​links in a global bond ​selloff due to its weak public finances and serial slippage on its deficit-reduction plans.

articles.title: Diesel prices top $6, setting new record
articles.summary: The average price of diesel in the U.S. hit a new record Friday, as the ongoing conflict with Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries strain the global energy supply. The average cost of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was up to around $6.05 on Friday morning, according to AAA. This marks…
articles.body:
The average price of diesel in the U.S. hit a new record Friday, as the ongoing conflict with Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries strain the global energy supply.

The average cost of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was up to around $6.05 on Friday morning, according to AAA . This marks a 63 percent cost increase from a year ago, when the price of a gallon of diesel was around $3.71. It is just less than a 14 percent increase from prices last month, when a gallon cost $5.32, according to AAA.

The rising diesel prices are expected to push up the price of everyday goods, as the fuel is commonly used by commercial delivery trucks for shipping.

Ukraine launched attacks this week targeting Russia’s vital oil sector. On Thursday, the Ukrainian military reported hitting a refinery in Siberia — causing fuel shortages in Russia.

Russia launched similar attacks on Ukrainian urban gas stations in retaliation.

The prices also come as the Strait of Hormuz — which transports roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil supply — has been significantly restricted for commercial traffic as the Middle East conflict persists.

The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian oil tankers earlier this week before Iran struck back Wednesday, launching attacks on 10 ships near the strait, including two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers, and strikes on a U.S. base in Jordan.

The disruption of traffic through the corridor has also caused the international Brent crude oil benchmark to hit $100.72 per barrel in early trading Wednesday, crossing $100 for the first time since late July.

While heading to the Republican National Committee’s first midterm convention , President Trump warned Wednesday that there were more attacks against Iran to be expected. He said the aim of the U.S. military operation is to prevent the country from building a nuclear weapon.

Trump added that he expects oil prices “to be tumbling downward” following November’s elections and after the conclusion of the war.

articles.title: Scammers target hundreds of thousands of crypto owners after Trezor confirms data breach of email provider | TechCrunch
articles.summary: This is the second data breach affecting a company that hardware crypto wallet maker Trezor relies on.
articles.body:
Hardware crypto wallet maker Trezor is warning customers for the second time in as many months that one of the companies it relies on was hacked, exposing the data of Trezor’s customers to hackers.

In a blog post this week , the hardware wallet maker said a cyberattack on Brevo, a marketing tech company that Trezor uses to send newsletters, allowed hackers to send around 347,000 phishing emails to Trezor customers with a malicious link purporting to come from the wallet maker.

The link, when tapped, downloads an app that asks the victim for their wallet backup password. According to Trezor, one of the email subject lines said: “Critical Security Alert: STM32 Entropy Vulnerability.”

With a stolen wallet password, a hacker can irreversibly steal the person’s funds on the public blockchain.

Brevo said in an incident status post that the hackers were able to access 138 Brevo accounts to send out the mass volume of phishing messages. Brevo said that the hackers abused a flaw that meant the hackers’ access was “not properly scoped.” The company said that the hackers’ access was “wrongly granted” to all organizations that the hackers’ accounts could reach.

The breach highlights a common security incident, where hackers compromise data held by third-party companies that are necessary for fulfilling orders or purchases from customers. Trezor says none of its products, wallets, or account system were affected by the incident.

This is the second breach in recent weeks affecting Trezor, after the company alerted customers in August that one of its shipping partners was compromised in a data breach . The incident at the mailing company ShipMonk exposed the names, phone numbers, email addresses, and postal addresses of at least 81,000 people who bought and received Trezor wallet hardware.

The data breach could put crypto owners and other wealthy individuals at risk of targeted violence and so-called “wrench” attacks , which rely on physical attacks to extract passwords from people.

In the weeks following the breach at ShipMonk, some people have received letters by mail claiming to be from Trezor, featuring a QR code that, when scanned, opens up a fake page that attempts to steal the victim’s crypto wallet password.

Trezor said it was reevaluating its relationships with its vendors and warned customers that their email addresses may be used again for future phishing attacks.

articles.title: Hassett Says Trump $5,000 Checks Can Be Fiscally Responsible
articles.summary: White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett played down concerns that President Donald Trump’s proposal to send $5,000 checks to every adult...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett played down concerns that President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 checks to every adult US citizen would add to worries about historically high government borrowing.

"We can do it in a fiscally responsible way," Hassett said in an interview Thursday with Bloomberg TV. "It is a serious proposal."

He argued that "because of all the growth and all the wealth being created in the US, the president thinks we need to return more of that to the American people." He said one way of doing that is via a reconciliation bill — a legislative mechanism that the majority party in the House and Senate can use for a fiscal package that bypasses the need for votes from the opposing party.

When pressed on what sort of offsets might be twinned with the checks — which would amount to more than $1 trillion in added spending at a time the US federal debt burden is heading toward a record high — Hassett said that would have to be "negotiated with Congress."

Trump floated the $5,000 proposal earlier this week, conditional on Republicans retaining their congressional majorities.

"The bottom line is there are multiple paths to getting it done — don't underestimate President Trump," Hassett said.

Analysts are skeptical the $5,000 payments will come to fruition, after top GOP lawmakers in the House and Senate offered a muted reaction to the idea.

"President Trump's attention-grabbing proposal for $5,000 checks to all adults if Republicans win the midterms is a non-starter in Congress, due to the massive fiscal cost and inflationary impacts," Evercore ISI analysts wrote in a note Friday.

The NEC director also on Friday said that while the August consumer price index release showed an acceleration in prices, the three-month trend still shows a deceleration in inflation. Asked about the potential for the Federal Reserve to react by raising interest rates next week, Hassett said, "I would guess that if the Fed makes a big move, the president will have something to say about it."

With assistance from Vonnie Quinn and Michael McKee.

articles.title: Fed rate hike odds surge to 90% on monthly jump in core prices
articles.summary: Markets are now betting on a 90% chance of a rate hike at Wednesday's Fed policy meeting.
articles.body:
A fresh reading on inflation showed monthly prices rose more than expected in August, increasing the likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week.

A rebound to oil at $100 per barrel also complicates the picture.

Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — the Consumer Price Index rose 0.3% month over month , compared with expectations for 0.2%. The year-over-year rate was in line with expectations for 2.4% and down a tenth of a percentage point from July. On a headline basis, CPI rose 3.4% in August, in line with expectations, and 0.4% month over month.

"The upside surprise to core CPI in August means the Fed looks set to hike next week," said Stephen Brown, North America chief economist for Capital Economics.

Markets are now betting on a 90% chance of a rate hike at Wednesday's Fed policy meeting, according to CME FedWatch .

Officials will use the latest inflation data to examine trends over the past three, six, and 12 months to assess whether price pressures are easing.

Fed officials have been divided about whether inflation is falling back down to their 2% goal on its own or whether they need to raise rates. Friday's data will fuel hawks like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack and Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan, who argue that inflation is broad-based and that without increasing rates, it won't come down on its own.

It may also not be enough to satisfy officials like Fed governor Chris Waller, who said last week that if August figures show inflation coming down and core prices staying at 0.2%, he would support holding rates steady next week.

"If there is continued progress toward our 2% goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level," Waller said on Sept. 3. "But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike. I judge that policy is currently only slightly restricting aggregate demand, and it may not take much acceleration in inflation to nudge me into supporting tighter policy."

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a speech at Jackson Hole, Wyo., last month that inflation is too high and that rates are not restricting borrowing in the economy, outside of housing. He noted that June and July inflation readings, which had shown some progress, hadn't been enough for him to mark the improvement he needs to see that inflation is coming down.

"Following a brief easing in June and July, inflation surged again in August which sets the stage for a likely interest rate hike," RSM chief economist Joseph Brusuelas said. He expects the Fed to hike at least two more times after next week over the next year to put inflation on a credible path back to 2%.

articles.title: Elon Musk dismisses Bernie Sanders's 5% wealth tax, says 99% of his trillion-dollar fortune is in stock — not cash
articles.summary: Most of America’s richest people are cash-poor, with wealth tied up in companies they helped succeed.
articles.body:
Elon Musk's elevation to trillionaire status this summer has been a PR nightmare for the already divisive figure, who has come to represent the elite, who many resent for accruing riches and wielding influence as the Americans face increasing socioeconomic insecurity .

To ease the worsening burden of the cost of living — and the large national debt — multiple levels of government have contemplated more taxation of the nation's highest earners in recent months.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

From Virginia's millionaire levy and Rhode Island's "Fair Share" duty on high-value assets to federal acts targeting billionaires, such as those pushed by lawmakers like Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren , "Tax the rich" has become a common call to action.

Sanders, for one, has singled out Musk specifically to drive home the need for the 5% charge the senator has suggested imposing on the ultra-wealthy.

While noting in a recent X post that the top 1% of wealthiest Americans now own an eye-popping $54 trillion in wealth — 468 times more than the bottom 50% of residents — he bemoaned that "One man, Elon Musk, owns more than the bottom half combined."

"This is what I mean when I talk about oligarchy," he wrote.

But, Musk was quick to clap back and argue that Sanders was missing the fact that most billionaires are relatively cash poor, with the vast majority of their funds tied up in ever-fluctuating assets like stocks. For Musk, stake in the companies he's built and helped succeed comprises more than a whopping 99% of his fortune .

As he retorted on X this week , "I have stock in SpaceX and Tesla, not some big pile of cash."

Musk has previously quantified his cash holdings as less than 0.1% of his total net worth , also pointing out that his employees receive stock options and thus benefit from increased valuations, too, as do retail investors such as pension funds that have a stake.

Billionaires like Mark Cuban and Jimmy Donaldson, who goes by Mr. Beast on YouTube, have echoed the same point, with the latter telling the Wall Street Journal earlier this year that he has "negative money right now" and is in fact "borrowing money, that's how little money I have."

articles.title: Fed’s Rate Decision May Have Come Down to Phone Plan Changes
articles.summary: A record jump in the price of cellular phone services helped tip a key measure of US inflation above forecasts, likely sealing the deal for a Federal Reserve...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A record jump in the price of cellular phone services helped tip a key measure of US inflation above forecasts, likely sealing the deal for a Federal Reserve interest-rate increase next week.

The consumer price index excluding food and energy climbed 0.3% in August from a month earlier, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data out Friday. The median estimate in a Bloomberg survey called for a 0.2% increase. The 5.9% surge in wireless telephone services prices alone added about a 10th of a percentage point to the core reading.

That gauge largely reflects prepaid and monthly plans offered by cellular carriers.

Economists at Bank of America Corp., Barclays Plc and Pantheon Macroeconomics flagged recent plan changes by major carriers like AT&T Inc. and T-Mobile US Inc. as likely culprits. The BLS declined to elaborate on how the changes at those carriers may have impacted the number.

AT&T said earlier this year that it would implement price increases on certain plans in August. T-Mobile also recently retired some of its legacy plans, resulting in price increases for consumers.

Even so, many Fed-watchers still saw a case for raising interest rates, even if underlying inflation was lifted last month partly by one-time factors.

"While it is true that the wireless index added 10bps to the core CPI today, and that the core ex-wireless would have been 0.20%, I don't think the Fed will have the luxury of slicing and dicing the data at the meeting next week," Omair Sharif, president of Inflation Insights LLC, said in a note.

articles.title: Trump, Hegseth tie Iran war to 9/11 in speech at Pentagon
articles.summary: President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth tied the Iran war to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in their anniversary remarks Friday at the Pentagon, suggesting the conflict is a continuation of the war on terror. “We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the…
articles.body:
President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth tied the Iran war to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in their anniversary remarks Friday at the Pentagon, suggesting the conflict is a continuation of the war on terror.

“We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said to claps from the audience at the ceremony.

Hegseth, speaking ahead of the president, said the U.S. remains “vigilant.”

“Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century, that cheered on 9/11,” he said. “A regime that has sponsored terrorist attacks against Americans for decades, killing thousands, including our comrades in Iraq and Afghanistan. But they did not factor in this president.”

“We’re still sending terrorists where they belong — to hell — and tankers to the bottom of the ocean, where they belong,” Hegseth added. “And we are ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

He reiterated that the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz and has destroyed Iran’s navy.

The global “war on terror” was declared shortly after the attacks in New York and lasted nearly 20 years, focusing on al Qaeda militants. The U.S. military withdrew from Afghanistan in August 2021.

Trump said earlier this week he sees the Iran war, which has already passed its six-month mark, lasting until the November midterm elections.

He said he thinks the war will “end immediately” after the election .

“They can’t hold out any longer,” Trump told reporters of Iran. “They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon.”

However, a Wall Street Journal report from Thursday said that Iran has resumed production of ballistic missiles, contradicting Trump administration claims that the country’s military capabilities have been destroyed.

The White House told The Hill that the U.S. “is watching Iran and has eyes on their every move.”

articles.title: The White House calls Truth Social the ‘most powerful and popular’ social media platform
articles.summary: The White House claims Truth Social “most powerful and popular social media platform in the world,” as YouTube and Facebook garner billions of monthly users each month.
articles.body: The White House claims the Donald Trump-owned Truth Social is the “most powerful and popular social media platform in the world.” The statement, provided to The New York Times by White House spokesperson Davis Ingle, is at odds with the user counts from some of the biggest social media platforms on the web. Data gathered by Search Engine Land shows YouTube is the most popular platform in the world, with 2.65 billion monthly active users. Facebook comes in second with 2.39 billion active users around the globe, followed by TikTok with 2.21 billion and Instagram with 1.99 billion. Truth Social doesn’t make Search Engine Land’s top 10 list, which shows Elon Musk’s X and Meta’s Threads at the bottom with 450 million and 223 million users, respectively. Even those platforms trail Pinterest, which is listed with 579 million global users. Truth Social’s traffic appears to be declining. As reported by the NYT, data from Similarweb suggests that the number of monthly visitors to Truth Social dipped 36 percent in July compared to the same time last year. From January to July 2025, an average of 28 million people visited Truth Social each month, while this number fell to 25 million during the first seven months of 2026, according to the NYT. Last month, Truth Social launched its $100,000 / month subscription to gain early access to posts from Trump and other prominent users, raising concerns about corruption. The NYT report details Trump’s posting patterns on Truth Social, which often include AI-generated images, such as one showing his head on Hulk Hogan’s body and another hitting a cut-out of Iran with a hammer brandishing the American flag. Ingle cites President Trump’s “authentic voice” as the reason for the platform’s so-called popularity, adding it’s where “he communicates directly with the American people and the world without the biased media taking him out of context.”

articles.title: Matt Mullenweg returns as Automattic CEO two days after getting booted
articles.summary: Two days after being placed on a paid leave of absence, Matt Mullenweg says he has been reinstated as CEO of Automattic, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch.
articles.body: Two days after being placed on a paid leave of absence, Matt Mullenweg says he has been reinstated as CEO of Automattic, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch. WordPress Executive Director Mary Hubbard confirmed Mullenweg’s return to the CEO role in a Friday post on X, which the official WordPress account shared and Mullenweg reposted. [Media: As 404 Media reported on Wednesday, Mullenweg had told staff in Slack that morning that CFO Mark Davies “conspired” with the board of directors, who voted to “put me on a paid leave of absence.” (Mullenweg said he voted against that.) He also told staff that the board had voted for Davies to become interim CEO. Davies, in a separate message, said that Mullenweg would still be a board member, according to 404 Media. An Automattic spokesperson told The Verge that Mullenweg was “currently on leave” from the company and confirmed Davies’ interim appointment. In the message viewed by TechCrunch, however, Mullenweg wrote that the board is “back in agreement” and that he’s “in control of Automattic.” He added that “A lot happened in the past 48 hours that we need to sort out, and I hope much of it was a misunderstanding, because I have huge respect and regard for those involved.” TechCrunch reports that Davies’ Slack account has been deactivated and that Mullenweg had removed “all” admins from Automattic’s Slack. 404 Media also reported on Mullenweg’s posts about his apparent return, saying he made the posts “late Thursday evening.” Automattic, which owns companies like Wordpress.com, Tumblr, and Beeper, didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge. At 12:20PM ET on Friday, Mullenweg posted on X that “If you don’t have a coup attempt every few years, you’re not hiring strong enough leaders,” adding in a separate post that “I think this was my fifth.” Mullenweg also published a blog post on Friday titled “Major Life Announcement” about making an offer to buy a houseboat. Updates, September 11th: Added 404 Media’s report and a post from WordPress’ executive director.

articles.title: Now recruiting: North Korea looks abroad for talent in its scheme to infiltrate U.S. companies
articles.summary: North Korea’s surreptitious push to plant employees in U.S. companies has expanded to include remote workers from other countries, such as Iran and Lebanon, according to U.S. government and foreign agencies and several cybersecurity researchers.
articles.body: North Korea’s surreptitious push to plant employees in U.S. companies has expanded to include remote workers from other countries, such as Iran and Lebanon, according to U.S. government and foreign agencies and several cybersecurity researchers. The scheme, estimated to involve thousands of workers applying to hundreds of American companies, generates hundreds of millions of dollars a year; the money is then laundered and used to fund the communist regime’s illicit weapons programs, according to U.S. government agencies. U.S. authorities and companies have taken steps to counter the ruse, which has in turn pushed North Korea to get more creative. In July, the State Department and the Department of Justice put out a joint warning with several foreign agencies noting that North Korea is employing “increasingly sophisticated” tactics, including recruiting individuals outside its own country to help “obfuscate their identities and expand their activities globally.” Government officials say North Korean teams are more frequently using people in foreign countries to participate as candidates in job interviews and sometimes establish in-person contact, in order to obtain work contracts. Once the job is secured, a North Korean agent typically takes over. Iran is part of a growing list of countries including Syria, Lebanon, South Africa and Saudi Arabia, that have recently been cited by researchers as countries where North Korean teams are actively enlisting people to conduct on-camera interviews with Western companies. North Korea has long relied on U.S-based facilitators to receive and run company laptops and provide local internet access, but these internationally based individuals represent an expansion of the scheme’s accomplices. According to a report from Flare, a cyber threat intelligence company, since 2024 at least 14 Iranians have been directly recruited by North Korean IT teams and at least two Iranians received formal offer letters from U.S. employers after successfully completing interview processes on behalf of applicants from North Korean IT teams. In one instance, a North Korean operator noted on internal tracking documents reviewed by Flare, that he’d contacted more than 50 Iranian engineers. It is not clear if operators accepted the roles offered to them. Chris d’Eon, a threat intelligence researcher at Flare and contributor to the report, said Iranians make compelling targets for the North Korean scheme. “From the North Korean operators’ perspective, this is a place where it is hard to get work internationally at a good price. It’s hard to do that sort of arbitrage with Western jobs and Western salaries,” he said. Mirroring Western recruitment norms, foreign targets in some cases were identified on LinkedIn, given onboarding instructions and offer letters from North Korean teams, and later paid in cryptocurrency. In some instances, recruits were offered $500 a month to serve as part-time “interview associates” and coached to use false identities, according to Flare’s analysis of leaked North Korean communications. “North Korea and Iran are very similar in that they’re sanctioned, and almost because of those sanctions, they have had to spend the last few decades developing their own science and technology education pipeline for their nuclear programs. So, there’s a lot of really highly educated STEM people in both North Korea and Iran for the exact same reason,” d’Eon said. North Korea’s remote work schemes have proliferated since the pandemic, placing workers at U.S. companies in order to funnel money back to the regime and, in some cases, steal sensitive information. Those workers’ salaries are used in part to evade sanctions and fund the regime’s illicit programs, including its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile efforts, according to U.S. government agencies. The United Nations estimates the schemes generate as much as $600 million annually, while the U.S. State Department-led sanctions monitoring assessment placed earnings for 2024 as high as $800 million. In response, Western organizations’ HR and security teams have made efforts to equip hiring managers with tools to identify red flags and potential fraud. Candidates are sometimes prompted to wave their hand in front of their face to check for the use of AI filters or to say something negative about North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un. Using people from other countries to perform interviews is a way around those checks. “It’s not a technical response to a problem; it’s now moving towards a physical response to a technical problem,” said Adrian Cheek, a senior cybercrime researcher at Flare who worked on Flare’s investigation. Research by Kudelski Security, a cybersecurity firm, also found North Korean IT workers are now delegating parts of the interview process to developers elsewhere in the world who can pose as candidates and sometimes assist in passing technical tests. In a 2026 investigation, Kudelski Security identified developers in Iran, Syria and South Africa who had accepted proposals from North Koreans after being approached on LinkedIn. Beyond on-camera interview roles, North Korean teams are increasingly subcontracting their work, specifically targeting developers with the necessary skillsets, as they manage multiple jobs at once and look to scale the scheme. Nigeria, Pakistan, India and parts of Latin America are also being targeted to assist in the scheme for facilitator recruitment, according to DTEX, a security company that tracks North Korea’s cybercrime. In response to the joint government alert on the expansion of the IT scheme issued in July, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry released a statement rejecting the advisory, calling it a “nothing but a stereotyped political accusation with a sinister purpose to tarnish the image of our state.” A ministry spokesperson added, “The DPRK will never allow any politically and ideologically motivated attempt of the U.S. and other hostile forces to use the cyber issue as the means of criticism and pressure on other countries.” North Korea doesn’t report economic data, but the Bank of Korea estimates North Korea’s real gross domestic product grew by 3.5% in 2025, marking the third consecutive year of growth over 3% in spite of global sanctions. Earnings from cyber crime are part of that growth, including IT work salaries and cryptocurrency heists, which net at least a billion each year, according to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

articles.title: Weight regain after diet pill use linked to rise in suicidal thoughts: Study
articles.summary: “It is likely to be connected in a complex way to the psychological and social elements related to failing to control one’s weight.”
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — People who used prescription weight loss medication and later regained the weight reported suicidal thoughts at more than four times the rate of people who never took the drugs, a new study found.

Researchers led by Dr. Son Ki-young, a family medicine professor at Asan Medical Center, analyzed data from 27,741 adults — 10,908 men and 16,833 women — who took part in a national health survey between 2013 and 2022.

Of those, 846 reported using prescription weight-loss drugs in the prior year, while 26,895 did not, according to the study published in Korean Journal of Family Practice .

Compared with people who hadn’t used the meds, those who had were 2.7 times more likely to report suicidal thoughts, 1.9 times more likely to report creating a plan and 1.7 times more likely to report an attempt.

They were also 1.9 times more likely to report depression lasting more than two weeks and twice as likely to have sought mental health counseling, the data shows.

The sharpest numbers came from a subgroup: people who took the medication and still gained weight.

Their odds of suicidal thoughts were 4.2 times higher than those who never used the drugs, while depression and counseling odds were roughly 1.9 and 1.8 times higher, the researchers found.

The study’s authors said the pattern likely reflects more than a direct drug effect.

“The increase in suicide-related index, among those who regained weight after weight-loss medication, is not just related to the neurological and psychiatric effects of the medicine itself,” the research team wrote, according to the International Business Times . “It is likely to be connected in a complex way to the psychological and social elements related to failing to control one’s weight.”

The study is observational, meaning it can’t prove the medications caused the mental health symptoms — only that a correlation exists.

The survey period also mostly predates widespread use of newer GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide (Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Zepbound, Mounjaro) in South Korea.

The sample instead largely reflects older appetite suppressants, including phentermine, diethylpropion, phendimetrazine, topiramate and orlistat — stimulant-based drugs already linked to anxiety, insomnia and mood changes.

People with severe obesity already have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body-image distress and a one-time survey can’t separate preexisting symptoms from new ones.

In January, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) asked drugmakers to remove suicidal-ideation warning language from the labels of Saxenda, Wegovy and Zepbound after a review of 91 placebo-controlled trials involving more than 107,000 patients found no increased risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior tied to GLP-1 drugs .

Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly both said they support the FDA’s findings, though Lilly’s consumer materials still direct patients to watch for mood changes and contact a doctor if symptoms are “new, worse or worry you.”

articles.title: Health officials declare end to largest cyclospora outbreak in history
articles.summary: The country’s largest outbreak of cyclosporiasis has ended, federal health officials said Friday. The foodborne illness linked to contaminated lettuce sickened 12,883 people across 21 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with more than 500 people hospitalized. Two people died in Michigan, which was the hardest-hit state, though health authorities…
articles.body:
The country’s largest outbreak of cyclosporiasis has ended, federal health officials said Friday.

The foodborne illness linked to contaminated lettuce sickened 12,883 people across 21 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with more than 500 people hospitalized. Two people died in Michigan, which was the hardest-hit state, though health authorities said they had “significant underlying health conditions.”

The lettuce, supplied by Taylor Farms in Mexico, is no longer available in stores or restaurants.

“At this time, there is no risk of people getting sick with cyclosporiasis from this source,” CDC wrote in the agency’s final update on the outbreak.

Once federal officials began linking the illnesses to Taylor Farms lettuce in mid-July, the company voluntarily recalled products from the market.

At the peak of the outbreak, before the recall, more than 1,000 infections occurred in a single day. Fewer than two infections per day on average occurred in August, CDC said. According to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), most of the illnesses tied to the outbreak began before the Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce recall was announced July 17.

The CDC is still investigating several case clusters of the parasitic illness nationwide. Including the multistate outbreak, CDC has received reports of 19,595 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis acquired in the United States.

The FDA said it is continuing its investigation into the outbreak, including how the product became contaminated with cyclospora. Last month, the agency sent inspectors to the Taylor Farms processing center and lettuce farms in northeastern Mexico.

In a letter to industry leaders, FDA’s acting deputy commissioner for food, Donald Prater, urged companies to invest more in cyclospora prevention and to follow food safety regulations.

Cyclospora is a difficult parasite to track, and the incubation period of illness can take up to two weeks after food is consumed, meaning people would need to remember what they ate weeks earlier. Lettuce is also a highly perishable food, so by the time a potential source is identified, consumers have often either eaten or thrown away the affected product.

articles.title: Asked Siri to call your bank? A scam could cost thousands
articles.summary: Asking Siri to call American Express connected an 82-year-old woman to a bogus number that nearly drained $100,000 from her Bank of America account.
articles.body: Asking Siri to call your credit card company sounds about as routine as asking for the weather. You say the company name, Siri finds a number and the call begins. For Virginia, an 82-year-old woman from Concord, Massachusetts, that simple request nearly turned into a financial nightmare. She says she asked Siri to call American Express. Instead, she reached a bogus number. From there, the conversation eventually moved to her Bank of America account and a supposed $1,000 credit that suddenly became $100,000. Virginia caught on before sending the money. Her story shows how a Siri bank scam can exploit something many of us barely think about: where a phone number came from before we dialed it. The Better Business Bureau has previously warned that fake customer service numbers can surface through voice searches. It has documented cases involving Siri and other voice assistants where people believed they had reached a legitimate company. Here's how the scam unfolded and what you can do before your next financial call to make sure you're reaching the real company. FTC REVEALS WHERE SPAM CALLS HIT HARDEST Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money Replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com Virginia's warning after a call she thought she could trust Virginia wrote to CyberGuy after the experience because she wanted other people to know how quickly a seemingly safe phone call can go wrong. "Hi, I just wanted to pass on this scam. I needed to call American Express. Instead of using the phone number on my credit card, I asked Siri to call American Express instead. It was all downhill from that point on. The telephone number was bogus, and eventually I wound up on my BOA account with a so-called BOA Security Expert. Fortunately, when zeros started being added to the $1000.00 credit I was supposed to get, and the "gentleman" said he couldn't correct it, I needed to go to BOA and return the $100000.00. I realized what was going on and immediately hung up and froze my BOA account. I never expected that a number that Siri provided would lead to trouble. I try to inform people now that calling a number can also put your finances in jeopardy. I am 82 years old and could have lost my entire retirement in one fell swoop. Thank you," Virginia, Concord, Massachusetts. That last part stopped me. Virginia had no reason to think asking Siri to place a call could potentially put her retirement savings in danger. After all, she initiated the call herself. That gave the person who answered an immediate advantage. How Virginia's Siri bank scam appears to have worked Based on Virginia's account, this looks like two scam techniques chained together. First came the fake customer service number. Then came a refund or overpayment scheme designed to persuade her to send real money back. Siri connected the call Virginia says she asked Siri to call American Express rather than using the phone number printed on her card. Apple says business information can appear across Apple services, including Maps and Siri. Place cards can include phone numbers and other business details. We reached out to Apple for comment but did not hear back before our deadline. However, Virginia's experience alone cannot tell us how this specific bogus number became associated with her request. We simply do not know how the bad number got there. The caller apparently posed as American Express This was a powerful setup because Virginia believed she had contacted American Express herself. She had not answered a random phone call. She had asked her iPhone to make the call. That can lower your guard before the person on the other end even says hello. The Better Business Bureau has warned about this problem. Scammers can promote fake support numbers that make their way into online search results. Voice assistants may then use information pulled from those results or related business listings. We have seen a similar trap with traditional web searches. In our report, The No. 1 Google search scam everyone falls for, a victim searching for customer support landed on a fake number and eventually lost control of his phone. Voice assistants can add another layer of trust because you may never see the number before the call starts. Then the conversation moved to Bank of America According to Virginia, she eventually found herself dealing with someone claiming to be a Bank of America security expert. At that point, the story had shifted from customer service to her bank account. That shift should immediately raise your guard. Bank of America warns about criminals who pose as bank representatives and invent urgent problems involving your account. Scammers may ask for verification codes, remote access or money transfers. Then Virginia encountered the clue that saved her. A $1,000 credit suddenly became $100,000 Virginia says she expected a $1,000 credit. Then zeros started appearing. Suddenly, she was dealing with $100,000. The supposed bank expert told her the mistake could not be corrected. According to Virginia, she was then told she needed to go to Bank of America and return the excess money. That follows a familiar overpayment or refund scam pattern. Scammers claim they accidentally sent too much money. Then they pressure you to return the difference before you have time to verify what happened. Fortunately, the sudden jump to $100,000 made Virginia question the entire story. She hung up and froze her Bank of America account. Did the $100,000 ever really appear in her account? We cannot determine that from Virginia's description. Scammers sometimes use remote-access software to manipulate what a person sees on a computer. They can also move a victim's own money between accounts, so it appears that a new deposit arrived. Another possibility involves a fake banking page designed to display whatever balance the criminal wants the victim to see. CyberGuy has covered how fake support representatives use remote access and other tactics to take control of devices. You can see the warning signs in our guide, Protect yourself from tech support scams. Virginia did not provide enough information to identify the exact technique used here. What we do know is that the criminal wanted her to believe $100,000 had appeared and that she needed to return it. If she had followed those instructions, the money she sent would have been very real. NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS Ways to protect yourself from fake customer service calls A scammer may know your name, your bank or details that make the call sound convincing. These steps can help you stay in control. 1) Use the number on your card For banks and credit card companies, the safest starting point is usually the number printed on the back of your physical card. You can also open the institution's official app and find its contact information there. Avoid relying on a phone number supplied by a search result, sponsored ad or voice assistant when your finances are involved. 2) Hang up when the conversation changes direction A call to your credit card company should not suddenly require you to move money through an unrelated bank account. If the story starts getting complicated, hang up. Then contact the company again using a verified number. 3) Never move money to 'protect' your account A scammer may claim your money needs to be transferred into another account to keep it safe. Do not do it. Bank of America warns that it will never ask customers to transfer money because fraud was detected on an account. The same caution applies if someone tells you to withdraw cash, buy gift cards or purchase cryptocurrency to resolve a banking problem. 4) Never return a surprise overpayment without verifying it If someone says $1,000 accidentally became $100,000, stop. Do not transfer the supposed difference back. Contact your bank independently and ask it to verify your actual balance and transaction history. 5) Never share one-time security codes Banks use one-time codes to confirm your identity or approve certain actions. A scammer may ask you to read one aloud while claiming it is needed to cancel fraud. Never give a verification code to someone who called you or someone you reached through an unverified number. 6) Do not install remote-access software for a stranger If someone claiming to represent a bank or credit card company tells you to install software that lets them see or control your screen, end the call. Remote-access programs can give criminals enormous control over your computer. They may watch you log into your bank, move money between accounts or manipulate what appears on the screen. 7) Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software can help protect you if a fake support representative sends you to a malicious website or convinces you to download a dangerous file. It can also warn you about phishing pages and other threats designed to steal passwords or financial information. The best way to safeguard yourself from malicious links that install malware, potentially accessing your private information, is to have antivirus software installed on all your devices. This protection can also alert you to phishing emails and ransomware scams, keeping your personal information and digital assets safe. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 8) Turn on bank and credit card alerts Set alerts for purchases, withdrawals and transfers so you know quickly when money moves. You should also enable notifications for suspicious logins and changes to your account information when your financial institution offers them. These alerts give you another chance to catch activity you did not authorize. 9) Use strong, unique passwords and two-factor authentication Your banking password should never be reused on another account. A password manager can create and store strong passwords so you do not have to remember them all. Also enable two-factor authentication whenever your bank supports it. An authenticator app or security key can provide stronger protection when available. 10) Verify unexpected account changes yourself If someone tells you money suddenly appeared in your account, do not rely on what they show you. Close the session. Open your bank's official app yourself or type the bank's website address directly into your browser. Then check your transactions independently. 11) Report incorrect business information If Siri or Apple Maps provides incorrect business information, you can report the listing to Apple. On an iPhone, open Maps > tap your picture or initials next to the search field > tap Reports > tap Report a New Issue > choose the appropriate option and follow the on-screen instructions. Fixing a bad listing may help prevent someone else from reaching the same number. APPLE’S $250M SIRI SETTLEMENT: ARE YOU OWED CASH? What to do if you already gave a scammer access If you think a scammer got access to your financial information, act quickly. End the contact Hang up and stop responding to texts, emails or calls from the person. Do not use a callback number they provided. Call your financial institution directly Use the number on your card or inside the official app. Tell the fraud department exactly what happened. Ask whether any transfers, new payees or other account changes need to be stopped. Lock or freeze affected accounts and cards Virginia froze her Bank of America account as soon as she realized something was wrong. Your bank may also allow you to lock a debit or credit card instantly through its app. Change exposed passwords If you entered a password while the scammer could see your screen, or you gave one away, change it from a trusted device. Change any other account that used the same or a similar password. Remove remote-access software If you installed a remote-control program at the scammer's direction, disconnect that computer from the internet. Remove the software and run a full antivirus scan before signing back into sensitive accounts. If you are unsure whether the device is clean, get help from a trusted computer professional before using it for banking again. Check for changes to your accounts Look for unfamiliar transactions, new payees and changes to your phone number or email address. Also check whether the scammer altered security settings or added a new device to the account. Freeze your credit if sensitive information was exposed If the scammer obtained your Social Security number or enough personal information to open accounts in your name, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open new credit in your name. Report the scam Report financial fraud to your bank immediately. You can also file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If money was transferred, contact the financial institution involved as soon as possible. Some transactions become much harder to recover once they are completed. Watch for follow-up scams Criminals may contact victims again after the first attempt. Sometimes they pretend to be investigators, bank employees or recovery specialists who claim they can get your money back. Treat any unexpected follow-up contact with suspicion. Kurt's key takeaways What sticks with me about Virginia's story is how ordinary the first move felt. She was trying to reach a company she already trusted and used Siri to save herself a little time. That tiny convenience nearly opened the door to a six-figure loss. Virginia also deserves credit for catching the moment when the story stopped making sense. A $1,000 credit becoming $100,000 was enough to make her question the person guiding her. That instinct protected her retirement. I also would not frame this as an age issue. Criminals succeed because they exploit trust in familiar technology and recognizable financial brands. Anyone can get caught when a call begins through a device they use every day. From now on, I would treat financial phone numbers almost like passwords. Verify them before you use them. The number on your physical card or inside the official banking app gives you a much stronger starting point than a search result or voice request. After hearing what happened to Virginia, would you still let Siri dial your bank without checking the number first? Have you ever reached the wrong company through a voice assistant or online search? articles.title: TikTok misled consumers about filtering content for minors, judge rules
articles.summary: A Texas judge on Thursday ruled the social media platform TikTok misled consumers about the company’s efforts to filter inappropriate content for minors. In her ruling, Texas District Judge Cory Liu said TikTok’s claims about its content-moderation policies violated the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. The state of Texas alleged TikTok did not remove certain…
articles.body:
A Texas judge on Thursday ruled the social media platform TikTok misled consumers about the company’s efforts to filter inappropriate content for minors.

In her ruling , Texas District Judge Cory Liu said TikTok’s claims about its content-moderation policies violated the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

The state of Texas alleged TikTok did not remove certain categories of videos, including sexually suggestive or graphic content or promotions of gambling or drugs, that violated the platform’s community guidelines.

The internal content-moderation policies, according to the state, “instructed that such content should be allowed to remain on the platform with the designation of ‘hard to find’ rather than ‘do not allow,'” court filings show.

The state also argued TikTok misled users when claiming its “Restricted Mode” effectively filtered out content potentially inappropriate for minors.

Prosecutors alleged TikTok employees internally acknowledged the restricted mode did not work as intended and “exposed users to a high amount of content that should have been filtered out,” the filing stated.

Liu ruled the state met the burden for summary judgment on both allegations, allowing the trial to move forward. The trial, which is expected to be set for next month, would mark the first full trial on safety claims for TikTok if a settlement is not reached beforehand.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) celebrated Liu’s ruling Thursday, writing TikTok “sacrificed the safety and innocence of children for engagement and numbers, and now they are being held accountable.”

TikTok did not respond to request for comment.

TikTok is among a handful of social media companies to face increasing pressure over its ability to protect children online.

The trial will follow two landmark verdicts earlier this year that found the social media giant Meta liable for its platforms’ impact on kids and teen mental and physical health.

Last month, Meta settled a similar case with nearly every state in the U.S., agreeing to pay more than $17 billion and roll out several platform changes. Texas was not part of this settlement, but revealed hours later it reached a separate agreement with Meta, bringing the company’s total sum to just over $18 billion.

In announcing the settlement, Meta specifically called out YouTube and TikTok to “join” the company in adopting what it calls a “new standard” for kids online safety.

In an open letter , Meta argued the benefits of its new standards will only be “truly effective” if other industry players follow the same standard, putting public pressure on its rivals to make a deal.

TikTok has largely stayed quiet, providing no public response to the letter.

articles.title: CIA releases never-before-seen warnings to Bush, Clinton about Al Qaeda
articles.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) on Friday publicly released for the first time a tranche of daily intelligence briefings provided ahead of September 11, 2001 to former Presidents George W. Bush and Bill Clinton about Al Qaeda’s plans to commit terrorist attacks on U.S. soil. The intelligence agency released 71 declassified documents in what CIA…
articles.body:
The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) on Friday publicly released for the first time a tranche of daily intelligence briefings provided ahead of September 11, 2001 to former Presidents George W. Bush and Bill Clinton about Al Qaeda’s plans to commit terrorist attacks on U.S. soil.

The intelligence agency released 71 declassified documents in what CIA Director John Ratcliffe called “an act of exceptional transparency” on the 25th anniversary of this tragic day. This is the single-largest release ever of the agency’s analysis of this terrorist attack, according to Ratcliffe.

“25 years ago, the 9/11 attacks struck a blow to our Nation, but they did not break us,” Ratcliffe said in a statement. “Generations of CIA officers have since dedicated their careers to securing justice for our fallen Americans and ensuring al-Qa’ida would never again harm our country.”

“In the years that followed, numerous CIA officers made the ultimate sacrifice in the Global War on Terror,” the CIA director continued. “We honor their memory and service through our commitment to disrupt, dismantle, and defeat those who wish to cause us harm.”

The files include a warning that Clinton received from the agency during his presidency in 1998. The memo , dated Sept. 10 of that year, warned that Al Qaeda “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a U.S. city.”

The 9/11 Commission noted this memo in its 2004 study but did not mention that it was included in the then-president’s daily briefing. Items in the commander in chief’s daily briefings are among the most sensitive documents and only circulated among the president and a small circle of national security advisers.

While these newly-declassified CIA documents do not appear to contain major revelations about these attacks, they do provide a window into the information these two commanders-in-chief received in the lead up to this tragic day.

Earlier on Friday, a 9/11 victim’s widow, Terry Strada, called on the Trump administration to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for these attacks during a remembrance ceremony in New York City.

Strada accused former presidents present at this event of withholding evidence and choosing to “protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families.”

“They broke promises, both public and private,” she said. “It has been one betrayal after another.”

Fifteen of Al Qaeda’s plane hijackers were Saudi nationals, and Strada and other family members of 9/11 victims believe the Saudis were complicit in these attacks — an accusation the kingdom has repeatedly denied.

The widow called on President Trump to “tell the Saudis to stop lying.”

“Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through,” Strada said.

The Hill has reached out to the White House regarding Strada’s request.

articles.title: Florida DMV says it was hacked shortly after major driver’s license breach
articles.summary: Florida’s Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles said Friday that it’s investigating a data breach, making it the second organization that hosts Americans’ driver’s license information to be hacked this month.
articles.body: Florida’s Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) said Friday that it’s investigating a data breach, making it the second organization that hosts Americans’ driver’s license information to be hacked this month. The Florida announcement comes on the heels of another incident, in which a vendor that scans Americans’ driver’s licenses for private companies, IDscan.net, said it was investigating a major data breach of its own. Hackers claimed to have stolen 160 million IDs from the company, including one from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, sparking federal investigations. While the two hacks do not appear to be related, they highlight how cybercriminals, whose jobs keep getting easier thanks to AI, can easily gain access to millions of Americans’ extremely sensitive personal information. Specifics of what was stolen from the FLHSMV are scant. But the department said in a statement published to its website that the breach was “conducted by an international cybercriminal organization.” Law enforcement is investigating the hack, the agency said, and the breach has since been contained. It’s unclear how long the hackers had access. Last week, ShinyHunters, a cybercriminal group that hacks targets for sensitive information and then extorts them for a payment to delete it, announced on its dark-web site that the “Florida DMV” was its latest victim. That website, viewed by NBC News, gave a deadline of Sept. 11 for Florida to negotiate a fee not to release hacked files. It included a single sample file, a screengrab of an image allegedly from Florida’s Driver and Vehicle Information Database, that showed the alleged driver’s license for late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, a former Florida resident. NBC News was unable to verify the authenticity of the image, which includes Epstein’s alleged Social Security number, former driver’s license number and vehicles registered in his name. On Friday afternoon, after the FLHSMV published its statement, ShinyHunters deleted references to Florida. It’s not clear why the posting was deleted in this instance, but Ian Gray, vice president of intelligence at the threat monitoring company Flashpoint, said that is often an indication that the state had reached out to the hackers to discuss a potential payment not to leak hacked information. “When a victim is missing from a blog, it typically means that there was a negotiation,” he said. The FLHSMV did not respond to questions on whether it was engaging with ShinyHunters. On Sept. 3, independent journalist Brian Krebs published an investigation that found a hacker group claimed to have hacked a driver’s license scanning company and was selling access to a tool that could access millions of Americans’ licenses. The company, IDscan.net, did not respond to requests for comment, but said on its website the next day that “an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud.” An FBI spokesperson confirmed to NBC News that the agency is investigating that breach.
